title: Lossless epoch stamps

blocks.text: An `Instant` holds nanoseconds, but `toEpochMilli()` **truncates** to whole milliseconds. For full precision the page reads `getEpochSecond()` and `getNano()`. Note that the nano part is always between 0 and 999,999,999, even before the epoch: half a second before the epoch is epoch second `-1` plus 500,000,000 nanoseconds.
A log format writes an instant as its time since the epoch in **decimal seconds with exactly nine decimal places**. Write `EpochStamp`:

items: `static String encode(Instant instant)` writes the stamp.
`static Instant decode(String stamp)` reads a stamp back into the same instant.

blocks.text: `java.math.BigDecimal` can hold such a number exactly.

cases.says: An instant after the epoch is written as its seconds with nine decimal places, and read back to the same instant.
Digits below the millisecond are written and read back, not dropped.
Five nanoseconds past a second is written .000000005, not .5.
Half a second before the epoch is written -0.500000000 and read back to that instant.

origin.section: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

concepts: An Instant keeps nanoseconds as epoch seconds plus a nano part, and toEpochMilli truncates to milliseconds.
An instant before the epoch has a negative epoch second and a nano part that is still between 0 and 999,999,999.
